You can't break anything here, and there are no silly questions. If something goes wrong, we start again.

replies.raw:
Basil loves warmth and sun. Here are the basics:

1. Give it a south-facing window with at least 6 hours of light a day.
2. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry — not before.
3. Pinch off any flowers as soon as you see them, so the plant keeps growing leaves.

Keep it away from cold drafts and air conditioning vents.

Notice how asking about your own basil got you a specific, useful answer — that's the chatbot working at its best.

It learned from a huge amount of writing, and it makes each answer by guessing, word by word, what fits best. It isn't a person, and it isn't a search engine.

[KEY]A chatbot guesses the best words to write back — it isn't looking up facts the way a search engine does.[/KEY]

There are many chatbots: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot. Merc is one too, and what you learn here works in all of them.

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 3] Teach me what I should never share with an AI chatbot, and why. Then let me practice asking for help safely.
replies.raw:
Last time, you asked a chatbot to say something in plain words.

Some things are safer to keep off the screen entirely. Think of it like a postcard: anyone could read it on the way to the mailbox.

Here's what to leave out when you type to a chatbot:

- Passwords and PINs
- One-time codes (the code a company texts you to log in)
- Bank or card numbers
- Social Security, Medicare or other ID numbers
- Medical records
- Photos of your ID, Medicare or insurance card
- Other people's private details

A general detail, like "I'm allergic to nuts", is fine. You can almost always get good help without the private part.

[KEY]Leave out passwords, ID numbers, card numbers and one-time codes when you type to a chatbot.[/KEY]

Try asking me: "My bank charged me twice. What should I do?"

replies.user: My bank charged me twice. What should I do?
replies.raw:
Here are the steps to take:

1. Call the number on the back of your card or on your statement. That's the real bank, not a number from a search or email.
2. Tell them the date and amount of the double charge.
3. Ask them to reverse the extra charge and give you a reference number for the call.

You can also check your bank's app or website to see if the charge is still "pending." Pending charges sometimes drop off on their own.

Notice that you didn't need your account number to get good help.

Your chats are usually saved, and some companies use them to improve their AI. To control this, look for the settings or privacy option in any chatbot app, or use a temporary chat if the app offers one.

The safest step is to leave private details out in the first place.

[EX]Google tells people who use Gemini not to type anything confidential they wouldn't want a reviewer to see. ChatGPT and Claude let people choose whether their chats help improve the AI.[/EX]

[Q]

A) "Is Rosebud1952 a strong password?"
B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
C) The code your bank texted you a minute ago, so it can explain it
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 4] Teach me about AI voice-clone and family emergency scams, and exactly what to do if I get one of those calls. Then help me make a plan.
replies.raw:
Last time, you learned the postcard rule.

AI can copy someone's voice from a short recording — even a video posted online. Scammers use that copy to call you, sounding exactly like a grandchild or other relative.

Even if their name or number shows on your screen, callers can fake that too.

Here are the warning signs:

- It's urgent.
- It's a secret ("don't tell Mom").
- They want cash, gift cards, or money sent from your bank.
- Some even send someone to your door to pick up cash.

[EX]In 2023, an Arizona mother got a call. Her 15-year-old daughter was safe the whole time. But a voice that sounded exactly like her daughter asked for help, and a man demanded money. The mother later told the U.S. Senate about it.[/EX]

A code word is a word only your family knows. If a caller can't say it, hang up.

Try asking me: "Write a text asking my family to pick a code word."
